rationale: Isaiah 49:24 asks, "Can the plunder be snatched from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be delivered?" and 49:25 answers, "Even the captives of the mighty will be taken away, and the plunder of the tyrant will be retrieved" (BSB). Matthew 12:29 pictures someone who "ties up the strong man" and then can "plunder his house" (BSB). The shared picture is taking plunder away from a strong captor. Four commentators on Matthew read on Biblehub make the link, at different strengths: the Expositor's Greek Testament, "The parable seems based on Isaiah 49:24-25"; the Pulpit Commentary, "there is probably a tacit reference to Isaiah 49:25"; Meyer, "The figurative language may have been suggested by a recollection of Isaiah 49:24 f."; and Gill, who glosses the strong man as the devil with "see Isaiah 49:24". Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Isaiah 49:24, reads the verse "Secondarily" of Satan and cites Matthew 12:29. The wording is not shared closely. In the Septuagint (Blue Letter Bible) the captor is a gigas ("giant") and the spoils are skula, with ischyontos ("one who is strong") in 49:25; Matthew has ischyros ("strong man"), skeue ("goods," BSB "possessions") and the verbs harpazo and diarpazo (the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus have diarpazo in both places). Only the root ischy- is common to both, and Luke 11:22, not Matthew, has skula. There is no citation formula, so the type is allusion, as with conn-matt9-blind-isaiah35. The label is plausible, not strong, because the overlap is one image and one word-root, and three of the commentators hedge ("seems", "probably", "may have been"); Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown do not.
